# Time-reversal symmetry

::: {.lecture-meta}
Lecture 3 · [Original notes](https://www.alucasphys.com/p7810s2026/p7810s2026_lecture3.pdf)
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives"}
Build a stochastic generator with a prescribed equilibrium distribution; derive detailed balance and fluctuation–dissipation; include variables odd under time reversal; and distinguish conservation on each trajectory from conservation only in the mean.
:::

## Build the generator from the steady state {#sec-l03-generator}

Suppose the equilibrium probability is $P_{\mathrm{eq}}=Z^{-1}e^{-\Phi(\mathbf x)}$, where $\Phi$ is a dimensionless thermodynamic potential. Define $\mu_i=\partial_i\Phi$. Write probability evolution as $\partial_tP=-\widehat W P$. Two requirements are immediate: total probability is conserved and $\widehat W e^{-\Phi}=0$.

A useful local Gaussian-noise generator satisfying both is

$$
\widehat W=-\partial_iQ_{ij}(\mathbf x)(\partial_j+\mu_j),
\qquad
\partial_tP=\partial_i\left[Q_{ij}(\partial_j+\mu_j)P\right].
$$ {#eq-l03-generator}

The derivatives act on everything to their right unless parentheses specify otherwise. The leftmost divergence guarantees normalization with decaying or reflecting boundaries; $(\partial_j+\mu_j)e^{-\Phi}=0$ guarantees stationarity. More general derivative expansions can be organized in the same way, subject to locality, topology, positivity, and boundary constraints. We will use the leading second-order operator rather than claim this factorization covers arbitrary nonlocal Markov processes.

The symmetric part $Q^{\mathrm S}=(Q+Q^{\mathsf T})/2$ controls diffusion and must be positive semidefinite. The antisymmetric part can generate reversible probability circulation. For general state-dependent coefficients, comparison with the Itô Fokker–Planck equation yields

$$
B_{ij}=Q_{ij}+Q_{ji},
\qquad
a_i=-Q_{ij}\mu_j+\partial_jQ_{ij}.
$$ {#eq-l03-drift}

The derivative term is essential for multiplicative noise. Equilibrium fixes a relation between drift and fluctuations, not merely a particular stationary solution.

## Reverse transition probabilities {#sec-l03-detailed-balance}

Let $G(x,t;y)$ be the probability density to reach $x$ from $y$ in time $t$. In operator notation,

$$
G(x,t;y)=\langle x|e^{-t\widehat W}|y\rangle.
$$

This resembles a quantum propagator, but stochastic evolution is neither unitary nor probability-amplitude evolution. Transposing the kernel exchanges initial and final states. Integration by parts gives $(\partial_i)^{\mathsf T}=-\partial_i$, so the equilibrium-weighted reverse generator is

$$
\widehat W_{\mathrm{rev}}=e^{-\Phi}\widehat W^{\mathsf T}e^{\Phi}
=-\partial_iQ_{ji}(\partial_j+\mu_j).
$$ {#eq-l03-reverse}

The reverse dynamics therefore transposes $Q$. The associated transition kernels satisfy

$$
G(x,t;y)e^{-\Phi(y)}
=G_{\mathrm{rev}}(y,t;x)e^{-\Phi(x)}.
$$ {#eq-l03-reverse-kernel}

If all coordinates are even under time reversal and $Q=Q^{\mathsf T}$, the forward and reverse generators agree. Equation @eq-l03-reverse-kernel then becomes **detailed balance**:

$$
G(x,t;y)P_{\mathrm{eq}}(y)=G(y,t;x)P_{\mathrm{eq}}(x).
$$ {#eq-l03-db}

This compares equilibrium-weighted histories. It does not say the conditional probabilities $G(x,t;y)$ and $G(y,t;x)$ are equal.

## Why detailed balance allows an arrow of time {#sec-l03-arrow}

Consider $dx=-\lambda xdt+\sigma dW$, with $\lambda>0$. Its equilibrium potential is $\Phi=\lambda x^2/\sigma^2$. If $x_0$ lies far outside the typical equilibrium width, relaxation from $x_0$ toward zero is likely. Detailed balance gives

$$
G(x_0,t;0)=G(0,t;x_0)e^{-\lambda x_0^2/\sigma^2}.
$$

The reverse fluctuation is possible but exponentially suppressed. A specially prepared atypical initial condition breaks the symmetry of the ensemble of histories even when the dynamical law satisfies detailed balance. Microscopic reversibility and macroscopic relaxation can coexist.

For an overdamped particle with potential $U$, choose $\Phi=U/T$ and $Q=T/\gamma$. Then @eq-l03-drift gives $a=-U'/\gamma$ and $B=2T/\gamma$. Equivalently, the random force covariance is $2\gamma T\delta(t-s)$. The fluctuation–dissipation relation follows from the same symmetric $Q$ appearing in both the restoring drift and the covariance.

### Supplemental derivation: a decreasing relative entropy

For symmetric positive $Q$, write $P=rP_{\mathrm{eq}}$ and define

$$
\mathcal D[P\Vert P_{\mathrm{eq}}]=\int dx\,P\log\frac{P}{P_{\mathrm{eq}}}.
$$

Since $(\partial_j+\mu_j)P=P\partial_j\log r$, integration by parts gives

$$
\frac{d\mathcal D}{dt}
=-\int dx\,P\,\partial_i\log r\,Q_{ij}\,\partial_j\log r\leq0.
$$ {#eq-l03-entropy}

Normalization removes the derivative of the extra constant in $\partial_t(P\log P)$. This inequality makes relaxation precise without requiring every individual history to have increasing entropy. Convergence to a unique equilibrium additionally needs ergodicity; conserved quantities can divide configuration space into disconnected sectors.

## Momentum is odd under time reversal {#sec-l03-odd}

Physical time reversal often transforms the state as well as reversing the order of events. Let $\Theta$ act by $x_i\mapsto\epsilon_i x_i$, with $\epsilon_i=\pm1$ and $\Theta^2=1$. For position and momentum, $\epsilon_x=+1$, $\epsilon_p=-1$. Assume $\Phi(\Theta x)=\Phi(x)$. The appropriate reverse generator is

$$
\widehat W_{\mathrm{rev}}=e^{-\Phi}\Theta\widehat W^{\mathsf T}\Theta e^{\Phi}.
$$ {#eq-l03-general-reverse}

Generalized detailed balance sets this equal to $\widehat W$. The relation between kernels now compares $y\to x$ with $\Theta x\to\Theta y$.

For a free particle with $\dot x=p/m$, $\dot p=0$, probability evolves by the Liouville equation

$$
\partial_tP+\partial_x\left(\frac p mP\right)=0.
$$

Transposition changes the sign of the streaming derivative; reversing $p$ changes it back. Hence free streaming is time-reversal symmetric even though the generator is not symmetric under ordinary transpose. This is why one must specify the parity of every slow variable before constraining a hydrodynamic theory.

## Strong and weak conservation {#sec-l03-conservation}

A stochastic system has two distinct conservation notions. **Strong conservation** means $F(x_t)$ remains constant on every realization. **Weak conservation** means only $\langle F(x_t)\rangle$ is constant for every initial ensemble.

For a diffusion, Itô's formula gives

$$
dF=\left(a_i\partial_iF+\frac12B_{ij}\partial_i\partial_jF\right)dt
+\partial_iF\,b_{i\alpha}dW_\alpha.
$$ {#eq-l03-dF}

Weak conservation requires the backward generator $\mathcal LF=0$. Strong conservation additionally requires every noise direction to be tangent to a surface of fixed $F$: $\partial_iF\,b_{i\alpha}=0$. In the forward-generator language used in the notes, strong conservation appears as

$$
[\widehat W,F]=0,
\qquad
e^{-\lambda F}\widehat W e^{\lambda F}=\widehat W,
$$ {#eq-l03-strong}

where $F$ denotes multiplication by the function. Conjugation shifts $\partial_i\mapsto\partial_i+\lambda\partial_iF$. This shift symmetry will become especially useful for response fields.

A worked two-particle example is

$$
\begin{aligned}
dp_1&=-\alpha(p_1-p_2)dt+\beta dW,\\
dp_2&=-\alpha(p_2-p_1)dt-\beta dW.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both the drift and the noise cancel in $d(p_1+p_2)$; total momentum is strongly conserved. Its forward generator uses only the derivative combination $\partial_{p_1}-\partial_{p_2}$, invariant under shifting both derivatives by the same constant.

If independent common noise $\gamma dV$ is added to **both** equations, then

$$
d(p_1+p_2)=2\gamma dV,
\quad
\frac{d\langle p_1+p_2\rangle}{dt}=0,
\quad
\frac{d\operatorname{Var}(p_1+p_2)}{dt}=4\gamma^2.
$$

This is weak conservation only. Hydrodynamic continuity equations require local conservation on each microscopic history, not merely the accidental constancy of a mean.

## Common pitfalls {#sec-l03-pitfalls}

Do not identify a stationary distribution with detailed balance: circulating currents can preserve a distribution. Do not omit the state-dependent drift in @eq-l03-drift. Finally, do not apply an even-variable time-reversal rule to momentum or spin, which are physically odd.

## Check your understanding {#sec-l03-exercises}

1. For a one-dimensional positive mobility $Q(x)$, find the Itô drift that preserves $P_{\mathrm{eq}}\propto e^{-\Phi}$ with zero current.
2. Does $dx=dW$ conserve $x$ strongly, weakly, or neither?
3. For the two-particle example without common noise, find the equation for $r=p_1-p_2$ and its stationary variance for $\alpha>0$.

::: {.callout-note title="Solutions" collapse="true"}
1. $a=Q'-Q\Phi'$ and $b^2=2Q$. Inserting these into $J=aP-\partial_x(QP)$ gives $J=-Q(\partial_x+\Phi')P$, which vanishes at equilibrium.
2. It conserves the mean of $x$ for any initial distribution with a finite mean, so conservation is weak. The variance grows and individual trajectories fluctuate.
3. $dr=-2\alpha rdt+2\beta dW$. The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck variance is $(2\beta)^2/(2\times2\alpha)=\beta^2/\alpha$; the conserved total momentum labels a separate sector.
:::
